claim: Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) leukemia is a fatal hematological malignancy.
source: Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) leukemia is a fatal hematological malignancy.
evidence: This is a general characterization of Ph+ leukemia presented in the abstract, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Standard treatments with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have achieved remarkable success in prolonging patient survival.
source: Although standard treatments with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have achieved remarkable success in prolonging patient survival, intolerance, relapse, and TKI resistance remain serious issues for patients with Ph+ leukemia.
evidence: This statement references established clinical knowledge about TKI treatment outcomes.

claim: Intolerance, relapse, and TKI resistance remain serious issues for patients with Ph+ leukemia.
source: Although standard treatments with tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have achieved remarkable success in prolonging patient survival, intolerance, relapse, and TKI resistance remain serious issues for patients with Ph+ leukemia.
evidence: This statement references known clinical challenges in Ph+ leukemia treatment.

claim: RAPSYN and BCR-ABL co-occur in Ph+ leukemia.
source: Here, we report a new leukemogenic process in which RAPSYN and BCR-ABL co-occur in Ph+ leukemia, and RAPSYN mediates the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: RAPSYN mediates the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
source: Here, we report a new leukemogenic process in which RAPSYN and BCR-ABL co-occur in Ph+ leukemia, and RAPSYN mediates the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Neddylated BCR-ABL enhances stability by competing its c-CBL-mediated degradation.
source: Consequently, neddylated BCR-ABL enhances the stability by competing its c-CBL-mediated degradation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: SRC phosphorylates RAPSYN to activate its NEDD8 E3 ligase activity.
source: Furthermore, SRC phosphorylates RAPSYN to activate its NEDD8 E3 ligase activity, promoting BCR-ABL stabilization and disease progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: SRC-mediated phosphorylation of RAPSYN promotes BCR-ABL stabilization and disease progression.
source: Furthermore, SRC phosphorylates RAPSYN to activate its NEDD8 E3 ligase activity, promoting BCR-ABL stabilization and disease progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: PROTAC-based degraders are ineffective in vivo.
source: Moreover, in contrast to in vivo ineffectiveness of PROTAC-based degraders, depletion of RAPSYN expression, or its ligase activity decreased BCR-ABL stability and, in turn, inhibited tumor formation and growth.
evidence: This statement references prior knowledge about PROTAC-based degraders discussed in the introduction.

claim: Depletion of RAPSYN expression decreased BCR-ABL stability and inhibited tumor formation and growth.
source: Moreover, in contrast to in vivo ineffectiveness of PROTAC-based degraders, depletion of RAPSYN expression, or its ligase activity decreased BCR-ABL stability and, in turn, inhibited tumor formation and growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) leukemia is characterized by the reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t (9;22) (q34.1; q11.2).
source: Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) leukemia is a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by the reciprocal translocation between the long arms of chromosomes 9 and 22, t (9;22) (q34.1; q11.2) (de Klein et al., 1982; Deininger et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The cytogenetic abnormality t(9;22) results in a BCR-ABL fusion gene.
source: This cytogenetic abnormality results in a BCR-ABL fusion gene, which encodes the chimeric protein BCR-ABL with enhanced tyrosine kinase activity (Cortes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BCR-ABL fusion gene encodes the chimeric protein BCR-ABL with enhanced tyrosine kinase activity.
source: This cytogenetic abnormality results in a BCR-ABL fusion gene, which encodes the chimeric protein BCR-ABL with enhanced tyrosine kinase activity (Cortes et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: BCR-ABL has been regarded as the most pivotal target for Ph+ leukemia therapy, especially for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
source: Based on its oncogenic role in Ph+ leukemia, BCR-ABL has been regarded as the most pivotal target for Ph+ leukemia therapy, especially for chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been the main treatment option for Ph+ leukemia, remarkably prolonging the patients' lifespan and improving their quality of life.
source: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) have been the main treatment option for Ph+ leukemia, remarkably prolonging the patients' lifespan and improving their quality of life (Hochhaus et al., 2020; Jabbour and Kantarjian, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Most patients develop TKI resistance and relapse after long-term treatment.
source: However, most patients develop TKI resistance and relapse after long-term treatment (Braun et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The increase of BCR-ABL expression can affect the sensitivity to TKIs and eventually determine the rate of TKI resistance in patients with Ph+ leukemia.
source: It is worth noting that the increase of BCR-ABL expression can affect the sensitivity to TKIs and eventually determine the rate of TKI resistance in patients with Ph+ leukemia in addition to the mutations in the kinase domain (Jabbour et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mutations in the kinase domain can change the conformation of BCR-ABL, thus interfering with the binding between TKIs and BCR-ABL and resulting in decreased therapeutic efficacy.
source: Mutations in the kinase domain can change the conformation of BCR-ABL, thus interfering with the binding between TKIs and BCR-ABL and resulting in decreased therapeutic efficacy (Lussana et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The increase of BCR-ABL expression can affect the sensitivity to TKIs and eventually determine the rate of disease progression and TKI resistance in patients with Ph+ leukemia.
source: In parallel, the increase of BCR-ABL expression can affect the sensitivity to TKIs and eventually determine the rate of disease progression and TKI resistance in patients with Ph+ leukemia (Barnes et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Effective degradation of BCR-ABL could address the issues on TKI resistance and leukemia-initiating cells (LICs).
source: Therefore, effective degradation of BCR-ABL could address the issues on TKI resistance and leukemia-initiating cells (LICs), and PROTAC-based protein degradation strategy may represent a new therapeutic approach (Békés et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the understanding of BCR-ABL's role in TKI resistance, supported by a citation.

claim: PROTAC-based protein degradation strategy may represent a new therapeutic approach.
source: Therefore, effective degradation of BCR-ABL could address the issues on TKI resistance and leukemia-initiating cells (LICs), and PROTAC-based protein degradation strategy may represent a new therapeutic approach (Békés et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PROTAC-based degraders at nM level have shown significant degradation of BCR-ABL in CML cell lines, cell lines carrying mutations in BCR-ABL as well as patient-derived primary cells containing multiple BCR-ABL mutations.
source: Currently, based on different ubiquitin E3 ligases, including VHL, CRBN, and IAP, PROTAC-based degraders at nM level have shown significant degradation of BCR-ABL in CML cell lines, cell lines carrying mutations in BCR-ABL as well as patient-derived primary cells containing multiple BCR-ABL mutations (Demizu et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2016; Shimokawa et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2019; Burslem et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The excellent cellular activity by the PROTAC-based degraders has not been able to translate to in vivo efficacy, even in rare examples of xenografted mouse models.
source: Unfortunately, the excellent cellular activity by the PROTAC-based degraders has not been able to translate to in vivo efficacy, even in rare examples of xenografted mouse models (Zhao et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 2021b), resulting in uncertain usefulness of these degraders.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The underlying mechanism of elevated BCR-ABL expression remains largely unclear.
source: Nonetheless, the unsatisfactory results are not really surprising because the underlying mechanism of elevated BCR-ABL expression remains largely unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: RAPSYN has been identified as a classic synaptic adaptor protein that binds to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) and several cytoskeleton-associated proteins, contributing to AChR clustering and neuromuscular junction formation.
source: Receptor-associated protein of the synapse (RAPSYN) has been identified as a classic synaptic adaptor protein that binds to the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) and several cytoskeleton-associated proteins, contributing to AChR clustering and neuromuscular junction formation (Huh and Fuhrer, 2002; Witzemann et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RAPSYN was found to exert NEDD8 E3 ligase activity to catalyze the neddylation for AChR aggregation.
source: Later, RAPSYN was found to exert NEDD8 E3 ligase activity to catalyze the neddylation for AChR aggregation (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RAPSYN was found to be located in the cytosol of the typical Ph+ leukemia cell line K562.
source: Previously, RAPSYN was found to be located in the cytosol of the typical Ph+ leukemia cell line K562 when a small molecule was used to probe its binding proteins using a proteomics approach (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Neddylation is sequentially catalyzed by the neuronal precursor cell-expressed developmentally downregulated protein 8 (NEDD8)-activating enzyme E1 (NAE1), NEDD8-conjugating enzyme E2 (UBE2M/UBC12 or UBE2F), and a substrate-specific NEDD8 E3 ligase.
source: As a type of post-translational modification (PTM), neddylation is sequentially catalyzed by the neuronal precursor cell-expressed developmentally downregulated protein 8 (NEDD8)-activating enzyme E1 (NAE1), NEDD8-conjugating enzyme E2 (UBE2M/UBC12 or UBE2F), and a substrate-specific NEDD8 E3 ligase to complete the covalent conjugation of NEDD8 to a lysine residue of its substrates (van der Veen and Ploegh, 2012; Enchev et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The neddylation of proteins can be reversed by deneddylases such as NEDP1.
source: The neddylation of proteins can be reversed by deneddylases such as NEDP1.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about neddylation.

claim: Accumulating evidence indicated the strong involvement of dysregulated neddylation in tumor progression, neurodegenerative and cardiac diseases, aberrant immunoregulation and others.
source: In the last two decades, accumulating evidence indicated the strong involvement of dysregulated neddylation in tumor progression, neurodegenerative and cardiac diseases, aberrant immunoregulation and others (Ying et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2020), which rationalizes the modulation of neddylation as a feasible therapeutic strategy.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: RAPSYN is highly expressed along with BCR-ABL in patients with Ph+ leukemia.
source: In this study, we report that RAPSYN is highly expressed along with BCR-ABL in patients with Ph+ leukemia and promotes disease progression, presumably by stabilizing the BCR-ABL fusion protein via neddylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: RAPSYN promotes disease progression by stabilizing the BCR-ABL fusion protein via neddylation.
source: In this study, we report that RAPSYN is highly expressed along with BCR-ABL in patients with Ph+ leukemia and promotes disease progression, presumably by stabilizing the BCR-ABL fusion protein via neddylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: The neddylation of BCR-ABL by RAPSYN subsequently competes its ubiquitination-dependent degradation to increase the stability of BCR-ABL.
source: The neddylation of BCR-ABL by RAPSYN subsequently competes its ubiquitination-dependent degradation to increase the stability of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: The NEDD8 E3 ligase activity of RAPSYN can be substantially increased by SRC-mediated phosphorylation.
source: Additionally, the NEDD8 E3 ligase activity of RAPSYN can be substantially increased by SRC-mediated phosphorylation, leading to enhanced stability and activity of RAPSYN.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: SRC-mediated phosphorylation of RAPSYN leads to enhanced stability and activity of RAPSYN.
source: Additionally, the NEDD8 E3 ligase activity of RAPSYN can be substantially increased by SRC-mediated phosphorylation, leading to enhanced stability and activity of RAPSYN.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: No difference of RAPSN mRNA levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was found between CML patients and healthy donors.
source: We analyzed mRNA levels of RAPSN in RNA-seq datasets of GSE13204, GSE13159, GSE138883, and GSE140385, and no difference of RAPSN mRNA levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) was found between CML patients and healthy donors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Neither a publicly available database nor our collection of patient samples and cell lines showed a significant increase in RAPSN mRNA levels.
source: Neither a publicly available database nor our collection of patient samples and cell lines showed a significant increase in mRNA levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C.

claim: The protein levels of RAPSYN were substantially elevated in the PBMCs of Ph+ CML (#8–11) and the bone marrow of ALL (#7) patient samples in comparison to that of healthy donors (#1–6).
source: The protein levels of RAPSYN were substantially elevated in the PBMCs of Ph+ CML (#8–11) and the bone marrow of ALL (#7) patient samples in comparison to that of healthy donors (#1–6), which was in a direct accordance with the expression of BCR-ABL (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The elevated RAPSYN protein levels were in a direct accordance with the expression of BCR-ABL.
source: The protein levels of RAPSYN were substantially elevated in the PBMCs of Ph+ CML (#8–11) and the bone marrow of ALL (#7) patient samples in comparison to that of healthy donors (#1–6), which was in a direct accordance with the expression of BCR-ABL (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Co-expression of RAPSYN and BCR-ABL was found in Ph+ cell lines.
source: This co-expression of RAPSYN and BCR-ABL was also found in Ph+ cell lines (Figure 1B), suggesting that the function of RAPSYN in Ph+ leukemia could be closely related to BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The function of RAPSYN in Ph+ leukemia could be closely related to BCR-ABL.
source: This co-expression of RAPSYN and BCR-ABL was also found in Ph+ cell lines (Figure 1B), suggesting that the function of RAPSYN in Ph+ leukemia could be closely related to BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-expression data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Notable cytotoxicity following marked reduction of RAPSYN was observed in all tested Ph+ leukemia cell lines and CML patient PBMCs.
source: Whereas notable cytotoxicity following marked reduction of RAPSYN was observed in all tested Ph+ leukemia cell lines and CML patient PBMCs (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), transduction with the shRNA for RAPSN did not affect cell viability of RAPSYN- and BCR-ABL-negative HS-5 cells, indicating the dependence on the presence and expression level of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 1C, D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Transduction with the shRNA for RAPSN did not affect cell viability of RAPSYN- and BCR-ABL-negative HS-5 cells.
source: Whereas notable cytotoxicity following marked reduction of RAPSYN was observed in all tested Ph+ leukemia cell lines and CML patient PBMCs (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), transduction with the shRNA for RAPSN did not affect cell viability of RAPSYN- and BCR-ABL-negative HS-5 cells, indicating the dependence on the presence and expression level of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is supported by cytotoxicity data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The cytotoxicity of RAPSN knockdown indicates the dependence on the presence and expression level of BCR-ABL.
source: Whereas notable cytotoxicity following marked reduction of RAPSYN was observed in all tested Ph+ leukemia cell lines and CML patient PBMCs (Figure 1C, D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F), transduction with the shRNA for RAPSN did not affect cell viability of RAPSYN- and BCR-ABL-negative HS-5 cells, indicating the dependence on the presence and expression level of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential cytotoxicity observed in BCR-ABL-positive versus BCR-ABL-negative cells.

claim: Exogenous expression of RAPSN rescued Ph+ leukemia cells from shRNA-generated toxicity.
source: Conversely, exogenous expression of RAPSN rescued Ph+ leukemia cells from shRNA-generated toxicity (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Knockdown of RAPSN changed the phenotypes of Ph+ leukemia cells, including proliferation, G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis.
source: Knockdown of RAPSN also changed the phenotypes of Ph+ leukemia cells, including proliferation, G0/G1 cell cycle arrest, and apoptosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G–I.

claim: Tumor growth was significantly inhibited by RAPSN silencing in a xenotransplantation mouse model.
source: Tumor growth was significantly inhibited by RAPSN silencing (Figure 1G, H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 1G, H, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1J.

claim: Immunoblotting of tumor samples showed a notable downregulation of RAPSYN expression, along with the reduction of BCR-ABL levels.
source: Meanwhile, immunoblotting of tumor samples showed a notable downregulation of RAPSYN expression, along with the reduction of BCR-ABL levels (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data from tumor samples shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The survival of tumor-bearing mice was profoundly prolonged by the knockout of RAPSN compared to the controls.
source: Consequently, the survival of tumor-bearing mice was profoundly prolonged by the knockout of RAPSN compared to the controls (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: RAPSYN is highly expressed at protein level with the accordance to BCR-ABL in Ph+ leukemia.
source: Altogether, our findings indicate that RAPSYN is highly expressed at protein level with the accordance to BCR-ABL in Ph+ leukemia and its depletion results in inhibiting the progression of Ph+ leukemia.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Depletion of RAPSYN results in inhibiting the progression of Ph+ leukemia.
source: Altogether, our findings indicate that RAPSYN is highly expressed at protein level with the accordance to BCR-ABL in Ph+ leukemia and its depletion results in inhibiting the progression of Ph+ leukemia.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Both nicotinic AChR subunit α7 and muscarinic AChR subtypes M2, M3, and M4 were involved in the cell proliferation of K562 cells.
source: Previous reports determined that both nicotinic AChR subunit α7 and muscarinic AChR subtypes M2, M3, and M4 were involved in the cell proliferation of K562 cells (Cabadak et al., 2011; Önder Narin et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: RAPSYN exerts its NEDD8 E3 ligase activity toward AChR in neuronal systems.
source: Furthermore, RAPSYN was found to exert its NEDD8 E3 ligase activity toward AChR in neuronal systems (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: No change in AChR neddylation was observed upon RAPSYN ablation in Ph+ leukemia cells.
source: Despite the expression of AChR subunits α7, M2, M3, and M4 at protein level in all tested Ph+ leukemia cells, no change in their neddylation was observed upon RAPSYN ablation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: No significant differences of neddylation-related genes (NAE1, UBE2M, NEDD8, and NEDP1) were found between CML patients and healthy donors.
source: In addition, we also examined mRNA levels of RAPSYN-related neddylation enzymes, including E1 (NAE1), E2 (UBE2M), NEDD8, and NEDP1, in above GSE databases, and no significant differences of these neddylation-related genes were found between CML patients and healthy donors as well (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Reciprocal immunoprecipitation revealed a strong interaction between RAPSYN and BCR-ABL in Ph+ leukemia cells.
source: To test this hypothesis, reciprocal immunoprecipitation was performed to reveal a strong interaction between RAPSYN and BCR-ABL in Ph+ leukemia cells (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Exogenous expression in HEK293T cells confirmed the specific interaction of RAPSYN with BCR-ABL.
source: Similar results were obtained with exogenous expression in HEK293T cells (Figure 2B), further confirming the specific interaction of RAPSYN with BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GST pull-down assay with purified proteins displayed specific binding of GST-tagged RAPSYN to His-tagged BCR-ABL.
source: Furthermore, GST pull-down assay with purified proteins displayed specific binding of GST-tagged RAPSYN to His-tagged BCR-ABL (Figure 2C), indicating that BCR-ABL is the primary target of RAPSYN-mediated neddylation.
evidence: This is supported by GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: BCR-ABL is the primary target of RAPSYN-mediated neddylation.
source: Furthermore, GST pull-down assay with purified proteins displayed specific binding of GST-tagged RAPSYN to His-tagged BCR-ABL (Figure 2C), indicating that BCR-ABL is the primary target of RAPSYN-mediated neddylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GST pull-down data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Δ1 domain (1–927 aa) of BCR-ABL was responsible for the interaction with RAPSYN.
source: Domain mapping revealed that the Δ1 domain (1–927 aa) of BCR-ABL was responsible for the interaction with RAPSYN (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by domain mapping data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Strong BCR-ABL neddylation could be detected in all Ph+ leukemia cell lines.
source: Next, we studied whether RAPSYN could directly mediate BCR-ABL neddylation. Strong BCR-ABL neddylation could be detected in all Ph+ leukemia cell lines (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The neddylation of BCR-ABL was validated by immunoprecipitation using the PBMCs from two CML patients.
source: More importantly, the neddylation of BCR-ABL was validated by immunoprecipitation using the PBMCs from two CML patients (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoprecipitation data from patient samples shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Treatment with the NAE1 inhibitor, MLN4924, significantly dampened the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
source: Treatment with the NAE1 inhibitor, MLN4924, significantly dampened the neddylation of BCR-ABL (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The mutation of two glycine residues at the C-terminus of NEDD8 required for its covalent conjugating ability essentially diminished the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
source: In addition, the mutation of two glycine residues at the C-terminus of NEDD8 required for its covalent conjugating ability, or the co-expression of NEDP1 (NEDD8-specific protease 1) essentially diminished the neddylation of BCR-ABL (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The co-expression of NEDP1 (NEDD8-specific protease 1) essentially diminished the neddylation of BCR-ABL.
source: In addition, the mutation of two glycine residues at the C-terminus of NEDD8 required for its covalent conjugating ability, or the co-expression of NEDP1 (NEDD8-specific protease 1) essentially diminished the neddylation of BCR-ABL (Figure 2H, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Mutation of Cys to Ala at the catalytic residue C366 significantly decreased the neddylation level of BCR-ABL.
source: As shown in Figure 2J, we co-expressed either WT-RAPSYN or its C366A mutant along with BCR-ABL and NEDD8, revealing that mutation of Cys to Ala at the catalytic residue C366 significantly decreased the neddylation level of BCR-ABL.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Knockout of RAPSN abrogated BCR-ABL neddylation in the cells.
source: Additionally, knockout of RAPSN abrogated BCR-ABL neddylation in the cells, and this effect was restored by transduction of RAPSN cDNA (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Transduction of RAPSN cDNA restored BCR-ABL neddylation in RAPSN knockout cells.
source: Additionally, knockout of RAPSN abrogated BCR-ABL neddylation in the cells, and this effect was restored by transduction of RAPSN cDNA (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: BCR-ABL could hardly be neddylated in the absence of RAPSYN in vitro.
source: These results were further corroborated by in vitro experiments, which showed that BCR-ABL could hardly be neddylated in the absence of RAPSYN (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro neddylation assay data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: The amount of neddylated BCR-ABL was markedly reduced in tumors generated by K562 cells transfected with shRAPSN#3.
source: Consistently, the amount of neddylated BCR-ABL was markedly reduced in tumors generated by K562 cells transfected with shRAPSN#3 (Figure 2M), indicating an essential role of the ligase activity of RAPSYN in BCR-ABL neddylation.
evidence: This is supported by immunoblotting data from tumor samples shown in Figure 2M.

claim: The ligase activity of RAPSYN plays an essential role in BCR-ABL neddylation.
source: Consistently, the amount of neddylated BCR-ABL was markedly reduced in tumors generated by K562 cells transfected with shRAPSN#3 (Figure 2M), indicating an essential role of the ligase activity of RAPSYN in BCR-ABL neddylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Neither overall BCR-ABL expression nor its neddylation levels were affected after the knockdown of AChRs.
source: In addition, neither overall BCR-ABL expression nor its neddylation levels were affected after the knockdown of AChRs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Modulation of AChR activities by either an agonist (carbachol) or antagonists (benzethonium and homatropine) did not alter the expression or neddylation status of BCR-ABL.
source: Similarly, modulation of AChR activities and their downstream PKC–RAS–ERK and JAK2–AKT signaling pathways (Kawamata et al., 2011; Aydın et al., 2013) by either an agonist (carbachol) (Jakubík et al., 2008) or antagonists (benzethonium and homatropine) (Durieux and Nietgen, 1997) did not alter the expression or neddylation status of BCR-ABL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H, I.

claim: Eight lysine residues were found to be potential NEDD8 accepting sites in BCR-ABL.
source: Subsequently, we tried to identified specific modification sites on BCR-ABL. The purified proteins were used for in vitro neddylation reactions, and the target bands were digested with trypsin for liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) analyses. Eight lysine residues were found to be potential NEDD8 accepting sites in BCR-ABL (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neddylation levels of BCR-ABL at candidate sites other than K257 were all significantly reduced, confirming the modification sites of these Lys residues.
source: To confirm these modification sites, a series of individual Lys-to-Arg mutants were generated. Except for K257, neddylation levels of BCR-ABL at other candidate sites were all significantly reduced, confirming the modification sites of these Lys residues (Figure 2N).
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Decreased neddylation of BCR-ABL following either MLN4924 treatment or RAPSN KO was accompanied by a strong decline in its overall protein expression level.
source: As decreased neddylation of BCR-ABL following either MLN4924 treatment or RAPSN KO was accompanied by a strong decline in its overall protein expression level (Figures 2G and 3A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1), we asked whether RAPSYN-mediated BCR-ABL neddylation affects protein stability.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2G, 3A, B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression levels of BCR-ABL declined much faster in cells with the induction of shRNA expression against RAPSN.
source: Subsequently, the protein synthesis inhibitor CHX was applied to K562 cells transduced with vectors encoding doxycycline-inducible RAPSN shRNA #3. Indeed, the expression levels of BCR-ABL declined much faster in cells with the induction of shRNA expression (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by protein stability assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A clear inverse correlation between the neddylation and ubiquitination levels of BCR-ABL was observed.
